docs.title: 2. Why Sim Race?
docs.text: Purpose: Make the case honestly — benefits and trade-offs — so readers self-select before spending money.

docs.title: Key points to cover
docs.text:
• Lower cost / lower risk than karting and track days (no tires, brakes, travel, damage)
  • Practice on demand: repeat a corner 50 times, race at night, any weather
  • Skill transfer: braking, racecraft, car control fundamentals
  • Structured competition: leagues, rating systems, esports pathways (overview only)
  • Social side: leagues, clubs, racing with friends (the F1 Arcade feeling, at home)
  • Cars/tracks you’d never otherwise drive

docs.title: The honest downsides
docs.text:
• Upfront cost and space (→ Where & When)
  • Time sink: practice, setup, tinkering
  • It’s a rabbit hole: “one more upgrade” (→ Buying Smart)
  • No g-forces / real-world risk feedback — manage expectations vs. real driving

docs.title: 3. Who Is This For?
docs.text: Purpose: A reality-check chapter. Help readers decide if sim racing fits their habits before they buy — and which tier matches how they’ll actually play.

docs.title: Key points to cover
docs.text:
• Two reader types:
  • Curious / casual: loved F1 Arcade, wants to test the hobby cheaply
  • Committed beginner: already knows they’ll race weekly and wants to skip a throwaway purchase
  • Questions to ask yourself:
  • Do you enjoy practice and gradual improvement, or only instant races?
  • Are you okay tweaking settings (FFB, FOV, bindings)?
  • How many hours per week, realistically?
  • Shared living space? Noise / vibration concerns?
  • PC, PlayStation, or Xbox already owned? (This constrains everything → How It Works)
  • Signs it’s probably not (yet) for you: no space, no patience for setup, expecting instant realism
  • “Buy once vs. buy twice” framing: when a cheap starter is smart, when it wastes money (→ Buying Smart)

docs.title: Pillar 2 — Controls (wheelbase + rim + pedals)
docs.text:

  • Rim = the steering wheel you hold (shape/size by car type)

docs.title: 9. Buying Smart
docs.text: Purpose: Help readers spend in the right order, avoid compatibility traps, and decide new vs. used — the chapter that saves people money.

docs.title: Buying order
docs.text:
• Proposed priority to validate in research: rigid mounting + pedals before raw wheelbase torque
  • What to buy first, what can wait (shifter, handbrake, button box, second rim)
  • “Skip-a-tier” math: when buying once is cheaper than upgrading twice

docs.title: Compatibility traps
docs.text:
• Platform licensing: PC vs. PlayStation vs. Xbox wheels/bases are not all interchangeable
  • Ecosystem lock-in: rims, quick releases, pedal connections per brand
  • Cockpit mounting patterns and torque limits (strong base on a weak stand)
  • Display/PC matching: triples and VR need a PC that can drive them

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
Purpose: One short, plain-language definition per term. Keep entries 1–3 lines and link back to the chapter that uses the term most.

Scaffold: definitions are placeholders to finalize in the research phase.

docs.title: Terms
docs.text:
Aluminum profile (8020) rig TODO — slotted extruded-aluminum cockpit frame; rigid and highly adjustable.

Clipping (FFB) TODO — force feedback signal maxing out and losing detail.

Direct drive TODO — wheelbase where the rim mounts directly to the motor shaft. See Components.

Ecosystem TODO — a brand’s compatible family of bases, rims, pedals, and accessories.

FOV (field of view) TODO — how much of the game world your display shows; should match screen size/distance.

Force feedback (FFB) TODO — forces through the wheel that communicate grip, bumps, and weight transfer.

Load-cell pedal TODO — brake pedal that measures pressure (force) rather than travel. See Components.

Nm (newton-metre) TODO — unit of torque for wheelbase strength ratings.

Potentiometer pedal TODO — pedal that measures travel/position; common on entry-level sets.

Quick release TODO — mechanism that lets you swap rims on a wheelbase quickly.

Rig / cockpit TODO — the frame + seat that holds the wheel, pedals, and sometimes displays.

Rim TODO — the steering wheel itself, separate from the wheelbase motor.

Simcade TODO — middle ground between arcade and full simulation handling.

Torque TODO — rotational force of the wheelbase; higher is not automatically better.

Wheelbase TODO — the motor unit that drives the rim and delivers force feedback.

docs.title: How components fit together
docs.text:
TODO: simple diagram — Platform → Wheelbase → Rim / Pedals → Cockpit; Display + PC alongside. See also How It Works — The 5 Pillars.

  • The wheelbase creates force feedback; the rim is what you hold and swap.
  • Pedals — especially the brake — are the biggest consistency upgrade.
  • The cockpit / mounting holds everything rigid; flex eats detail.
  • Displays / VR decide immersion, space, and how powerful a PC you need.
  • Shifters, handbrakes, and accessories are usually add-later items.

docs.title: Quick Start — 5-Minute Guide
docs.text:
Prices checked: 2026-10-02, US USD — volatile, re-check before buying

Summary layer: Totals use the same anchor prices as Example Builds — do not edit one without the other.

docs.title: The 6 decisions, in order
docs.text:
1. What do you want to drive? — track, rally, drift, trucking, sandbox… see Disciplines. This decides rim, pedals, shifter and seating position.
  2. Platform — PC, PS5, or Xbox Series X|S? Console licensing is the #1 trap.
  3. Space — desk only, fold away, or fixed corner/room?
  4. Seating position — Formula (reclined) vs GT (upright-ish) vs rally/truck upright. Pick by primary discipline; GT is the best all-rounder.
  5. Budget — gear only, assuming existing PC/console + TV unless a build says otherwise.
  6. Tier & build — Tier 0–5 below, then the linked build page.

docs.title: 5-minute summary
docs.text: Question Short answer What did F1 Arcade give you home gear won't at first? Full-motion seat, huge screen, zero setup, social head-to-head. Tier 0–1 will feel less spectacular; Tier 2+ beats it on force-feedback detail, braking consistency and seat time. Standard racing at F1 Arcade Chicago (1 W Grand Ave, opened Aug 2026, 61 full-motion sims) starts ~$19/session Cheapest real start $339–350 for wheel+pedals clamped to a desk (Tier 0) if you own PC/PS5/Xbox + TV/monitor Upgrade that makes you faster Load-cell brake, not more torque. From ~$149–160 (Moza SR-P2 / Logitech RS Pedals) The trap Console licensing. PS chip lives in wheelbase; Xbox chip in rim (Fanatec) or separate SKU. Moza/Simagic/Simucube/Asetek (except Moza R3-Xbox) are PC-only Sweet spot Tier 2 ($1,459, existing PC) or Tier 3 ($1,998, existing PC) Need a gaming PC? For iRacing, triples, VR, AC mods, LMU. PS5 = GT7 + ACC + F1 only, no triples/iRacing
